name: Bell-Szekeres Colliding Electromagnetic Waves
description: Two plane electromagnetic shock waves colliding head on in flat space. Where both have passed the spacetime is locally the Bertotti-Robinson universe, and the waves focus each other onto a Killing-Cauchy horizon with the curvature finite everywhere.
convention: No coordinate carries dimensions of time, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: Can two beams of light collide? Maxwell's equations are linear, so the two fields pass straight through one another, and the waves can only interact through the gravitational field of their own energy [griffiths1991]. P. Bell and Peter Szekeres worked the collision out exactly in 1974 for two plane electromagnetic waves with aligned polarizations, each one a step: nothing ahead of its front and a constant field behind [bell1974, griffiths1991]. Ahead of both waves spacetime is flat, and behind the wave of strength $a$ alone the metric is $-2\,du\,dv + \cos^2(au)(dx^2 + dy^2)$, conformally flat, with a fold singularity at $u = \pi/(2a)$ where the curvature is still finite [griffiths1991, feinstein1995, dorca1998].¶Where both waves have passed, $u > 0$ and $v > 0$, the metric is $-2\,du\,dv + \cos^2(au - bv)dx^2 + \cos^2(au + bv)dy^2$ [bell1974, griffiths1991]. Bruno Bertotti and Ivor Robinson had each found this geometry in 1959, in other coordinates, as the universe of a uniform electromagnetic field [bertotti1959, robinson1959, griffiths1991]. Between the two fronts sits a uniform electric field on the product of an anti-de Sitter space of two dimensions and a sphere, both of radius $1/\sqrt{2ab}$ [feinstein1995]. The region is conformally flat, and the collision radiates gravitational waves along its two boundaries, as impulsive waves, $\Psi_4 = -a\tan(bv)\,\delta(u)\Theta(v)$ on one and $\Psi_0 = -b\tan(au)\,\delta(v)\Theta(u)$ on the other [griffiths1991].¶Bell and Szekeres showed that for electromagnetic shock waves "the continuity conditions of Lichnerowicz must generally be relaxed in favour of the O'Brien-Synge conditions", and that two colliding shocks then produce gravitational impulse waves [bell1974]. They then compared the effect of such an impulse on a measuring device with the experimental results of Joseph Weber [bell1974]. Tilting the polarization of one wave against the other leaves the gravitational field the same: by the theorem of N. Tariq and B. O. J. Tupper the interaction region must again be the Bertotti-Robinson universe, and a rotation of $x$ and $y$ through half the angle between the polarizations brings its metric back to Bell and Szekeres's [griffiths1991, tariq1974].¶The two impulsive gravitational waves of K. A. Khan and Roger Penrose, in 1971, had focused each other into a spacelike curvature singularity [khan1971]. Bell and Szekeres's waves focus each other too, on the surface $au + bv = \pi/2$ where $g_{yy}$ vanishes, yet the curvature tensor stays bounded there, and the surface is a Killing-Cauchy horizon [griffiths1991, feinstein1995]. Bell and Szekeres removed the coordinate singularity with $T = -\cos(au + bv)\cosh ky$ and $Z = \cos(au + bv)\sinh ky$, where $k = \sqrt{2ab}$ [griffiths1991]. Richard Matzner and Frank Tipler argued in 1984 that "the apparently local curvature singularities both in the Khan-Penrose solution and in the Bell-Szekeres solution are actually global" [matzner1984]. Chris Clarke and Sean Hayward worked out the global structure in 1989: apart from the impulsive waves themselves the solution has no curvature singularities, and the two singularities left, at $au - bv = \pm\pi/2$ where the horizon meets the fold singularity behind each wave, are quasiregular [clarke1989, griffiths1991].¶Clarke and Hayward also carried the spacetime through the horizon, and found that the continuation is not unique [griffiths1991]. In one extension the waves cross and focus, and the spacetime that follows is unchanging [griffiths1991]. In another, in Jerry Griffiths's words, "the waves cross, mutually focus each other, re-expand and then separate leaving Minkowski space between them to the future" [griffiths1991].¶Is the horizon stable? Ulvi Yurtsever showed in 1987 that Killing-Cauchy horizons in plane symmetric spacetimes are unstable against plane symmetric perturbations [yurtsever1987]. Subrahmanyan Chandrasekhar and Basilis Xanthopoulos perturbed the whole spacetime in 1988 and found, between the fronts, a complete set of bounded normal modes written in spin weighted spherical harmonics, with a frequency that grows without limit toward the horizon [chandrasekhar1988]. Behind each wave alone the perturbations diverge along the entire fold singularity, which in their words raises "some serious conceptual questions" [chandrasekhar1988]. Deborah Konkowski and Thomas Helliwell sent test scalar waves through the Bell-Szekeres spacetime in 1991, found their stress tensor diverging at the quasiregular singularities, and argued that the divergence converts them into scalar curvature singularities [konkowski1991].¶Alexander Feinstein and Miguel Angel Pérez Sebastián quantized a massless scalar field on the spacetime in 1995, with Kruskal-Szekeres coordinates of the kind Miquel Dorca and Enric Verdaguer introduced in 1993 for the Killing-Cauchy horizon of two colliding gravitational waves [feinstein1995, dorca1993]. An observer at the horizon counts particles in the vacuum of the flat region, with a spectrum consistent at long wavelengths with a temperature $\hbar c\sqrt{2ab}/(2\pi k_B)$ [feinstein1995]. Dorca computed the stress tensor of such a field in 1998 and found it unbounded as the horizon is approached [dorca1998]. In more than four dimensions the same collision is no longer conformally flat and ends in curvature singularities, as Metin Gürses, Y. İpekoğlu, Atalay Karasu, and Çetin Şentürk found in 2003 [gurses2003].

related.text: Where both waves have passed, the metric is that of the Bertotti-Robinson universe in other coordinates, with $1/\sqrt{2ab}$ for the radius of both factors and $x$ running along its circle of longitude without closing [griffiths1991, feinstein1995].

Khan and Penrose collide two impulsive gravitational waves in the same four regions, flat space, one wave, the other wave, and both, and their waves focus each other onto a curvature singularity [khan1971, griffiths1991].

Behind either wave alone the spacetime is a plane electromagnetic wave, the pp-wave with $H = -a^2\Theta(u)(x^2 + y^2)$ in Brinkmann's coordinates, which Bell and Szekeres's chart writes as $-2\,du\,dv + \cos^2(au)(dx^2 + dy^2)$ [griffiths1991].
Ahead of both waves, where $u < 0$ and $v < 0$, the spacetime is flat [griffiths1991].

coordinates.name: Double Null

parameters.description: Strength of the wave that crosses $u = 0$, an inverse length: behind that wave alone the null rays across its front meet at $u = \pi/(2a)$
Strength of the wave that crosses $v = 0$, an inverse length: behind that wave alone the null rays across its front meet at $v = \pi/(2b)$

coordinates.convention: We use null coordinates $(u, v, x, y)$ where both waves have passed, all four of them lengths, with $x$ and $y$ across the wave fronts. Ahead of one wave or both, where $u < 0$ or $v < 0$, the metric is this one with $u$ or $v$ set to zero.
geodesics: \ddot{u} + b\sin\left(a\,u - b\,v\right)\cos\left(a\,u - b\,v\right)\dot{x}^2 - b\sin\left(a\,u + b\,v\right)\cos\left(a\,u + b\,v\right)\dot{y}^2 = 0
\ddot{v} - a\sin\left(a\,u - b\,v\right)\cos\left(a\,u - b\,v\right)\dot{x}^2 - a\sin\left(a\,u + b\,v\right)\cos\left(a\,u + b\,v\right)\dot{y}^2 = 0

coordinates.name: Time and Space

parameters.description: Strength of the wave that crosses $u = 0$, an inverse length
Strength of the wave that crosses $v = 0$, an inverse length; $1/\sqrt{2ab}$ is the radius of both factors of the product AdS$_2 \times$ S$^2$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(\xi, \eta, x, y)$ where both waves have passed, with $\xi = au + bv$ and $\eta = bv - au$ dimensionless, and $x$ and $y$ lengths across the wave fronts.

coordinates.name: Regular
domains: T^2 - Z^2 \le X^2 + Y^2 \;\text{(behind both wave fronts)}

parameters.description: Strength of the wave that crosses $u = 0$, an inverse length
Strength of the wave that crosses $v = 0$, an inverse length; $1/\sqrt{2ab}$ is the radius of both factors of the product AdS$_2 \times$ S$^2$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(T, Z, X, Y)$, all dimensionless. With $\xi = au + bv$, $\eta = bv - au$, and $k = \sqrt{2ab}$ they are $T = -\cos\xi\cosh ky$, $Z = \cos\xi\sinh ky$, $X = \cos\eta\cos kx$, and $Y = \cos\eta\sin kx$, one to one for $-\pi < kx \le \pi$ on either side of $\eta = 0$.
coordinates.line_element: ds^2 = \dfrac{-\left(1 + Z^2\right)dT^2 + 2TZ\,dT\,dZ + \left(1 - T^2\right)dZ^2}{2ab\left(1 - T^2 + Z^2\right)} + \dfrac{\left(1 - Y^2\right)dX^2 + 2XY\,dX\,dY + \left(1 - X^2\right)dY^2}{2ab\left(1 - X^2 - Y^2\right)}
geodesics: \ddot{T} + \dfrac{T\left(1 + Z^2\right)}{1 - T^2 + Z^2}\dot{T}^2 - \dfrac{2T^2\,Z}{1 - T^2 + Z^2}\dot{T}\dot{Z} - \dfrac{T\left(1 - T^2\right)}{1 - T^2 + Z^2}\dot{Z}^2 = 0
\ddot{Z} + \dfrac{Z\left(1 + Z^2\right)}{1 - T^2 + Z^2}\dot{T}^2 - \dfrac{2T\,Z^2}{1 - T^2 + Z^2}\dot{T}\dot{Z} - \dfrac{Z\left(1 - T^2\right)}{1 - T^2 + Z^2}\dot{Z}^2 = 0
\ddot{X} + \dfrac{X\left(1 - Y^2\right)}{1 - X^2 - Y^2}\dot{X}^2 + \dfrac{2X^2\,Y}{1 - X^2 - Y^2}\dot{X}\dot{Y} + \dfrac{X\left(1 - X^2\right)}{1 - X^2 - Y^2}\dot{Y}^2 = 0
\ddot{Y} + \dfrac{Y\left(1 - Y^2\right)}{1 - X^2 - Y^2}\dot{X}^2 + \dfrac{2X\,Y^2}{1 - X^2 - Y^2}\dot{X}\dot{Y} + \dfrac{Y\left(1 - X^2\right)}{1 - X^2 - Y^2}\dot{Y}^2 = 0

coordinates.name: Global

parameters.description: Strength of the wave that crosses $u = 0$, an inverse length
Strength of the wave that crosses $v = 0$, an inverse length; $1/\sqrt{2ab}$ is the radius of both factors of the product AdS$_2 \times$ S$^2$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(\chi, \rho, \theta, \phi)$, all dimensionless. With $\xi = au + bv$ and $k = \sqrt{2ab}$ they are $\sinh\rho = \cos\xi\sinh ky$, $\sin\chi = -\cos\xi\cosh ky/\cosh\rho$, $\theta = \pi/2 + au - bv$, and $\phi = kx$, and $\phi$ runs over the whole line.

coordinates.name: Kruskal-Szekeres

parameters.description: Strength of the wave that crosses $u = 0$, an inverse length
Strength of the wave that crosses $v = 0$, an inverse length; $1/\sqrt{2ab}$ is the radius of both factors of the product AdS$_2 \times$ S$^2$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(U, V, \eta, x)$, with $U$, $V$, and $x$ lengths and $\eta = bv - au$ dimensionless. With $q = 1/\sqrt{2ab}$ and $\xi = au + bv$, the null coordinates are $U = -q\,e^{y/q}\cos\xi/(1 + \sin\xi)$ and $V = -q\,e^{-y/q}\cos\xi/(1 + \sin\xi)$, so $2abUV = (1 - \sin\xi)/(1 + \sin\xi)$.

coordinates.name: Bertotti-Robinson

parameters.description: Strength of the wave that crosses $u = 0$, an inverse length
Strength of the wave that crosses $v = 0$, an inverse length; $1/\sqrt{2ab}$ is the radius of both factors of the product AdS$_2 \times$ S$^2$, the $b$ of the Bertotti-Robinson universe

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, all dimensionless. With $q = 1/\sqrt{2ab}$ they are $t = e^{y/q}\tan(au + bv)$, $r = e^{y/q}\sec(au + bv)$, $\theta = \pi/2 + au - bv$, and $\phi = x/q$, and $\phi$ runs over the whole line.
